name: Wakeout
summary: Wakeout is built around one running measure, Wakeout Watts, that a completed movement break adds to and a daily goal converts into a recognized state. Reaching that goal triggers a celebration and advances a running streak in the same moment, so one action moves three parts of the system at once. There is no free tier: every mechanic described here sits behind the subscription, with no version of the app to try first.
teaser: Wakeout can pause other apps on the phone until the user completes a movement break, a mechanic that sits in settings and is never surfaced during onboarding.

writeup.observed: Wakeout turns movement into Wakeout Watts, a single number we grow toward a daily target rather than toward any one finish line. The main action is completing a wakeout, a movement break, and what the app offers are four 15-second exercises. Completing one added 50 watts in a pop up naming the move we had just finished, and our running total moved from 613 to 663 in the same moment. The daily target is not fixed. Wakeout lets the user pick a difficulty level, and each level sets two numbers: an active goal and a stretch goal above it. On easy, the default, that is 500 and 200 watts, with earning capped at 150 watts an hour. The app's own copy frames the cap as encouraging movement across the day rather than one intense session. Harder levels raise both numbers. The total also persists beyond the day, tracked as a weekly figure and a single-day high in a dedicated stats section, with an hourly log behind it breaking down what produced the watts.
writeup.presented: The running total sits at the top of the home screen as a number against the day's target, above a bar that fills toward it. A check mark partway along marks the active goal, and the bar keeps filling past that point toward the stretch target. The same number reappears in the pop up after every completed move, in a calendar on the progress screen, and in the watts stats and activity log.
writeup.noting: Wakeout keeps the watts moving toward the day's threshold and nowhere else, and the hourly cap works on the same principle: it slows how fast the total can climb rather than blocking any single action, keeping the pressure on spreading movement through the day instead of finishing it in one sitting. Five difficulty levels turn the same design into five different daily targets rather than five different mechanics, so we change how hard the goal is to reach without changing what reaching it means.
findings: A completed move adds a fixed 50 watts to the running total, shown in the same pop up that names the move.
Five difficulty levels each pair an active goal with a stretch goal above it, easy setting them at 500 and 200 watts.
The easy default caps earning at 150 watts an hour, limiting how much of the day's target one burst of activity can fill.
The running total is also kept as a longer record, with a weekly figure and a single day high shown in a dedicated stats section.

writeup.observed: Wakeout counts a streak of days on which we reached the daily watts goal, sitting beside the goal total rather than tracking its own separate action. After the goal was reached, the app recorded a one-day streak, shown on the home screen next to the watts total, and a section on the progress screen headed "activity goal streak, reach your goal, increase your streak" kept the same count alongside a calendar and a longest streak record. We reached it through a gym session recorded that day, not through completing a wakeout inside the app itself. Settings also carries a control described as "take a day off," which turns off notifications for a chosen number of days under copy reading "don't break your streak."
writeup.presented: The streak count sits at the top of the home screen beside the watts total, and reappears inside the activity goal streak section on the progress screen and as a longest streak figure in the watts stats. The day off control sits in settings, framed around protecting the streak rather than around notifications alone.
writeup.noting: The qualifying event for the streak is reaching the day's watts goal, the same event Wakeout already celebrates on its own, so the streak adds a cumulative layer on top of a threshold that is already being tracked rather than asking for a separate action. Framing the day off control around not breaking the streak, rather than only around muting notifications, keeps the streak named as the thing being protected, as with the watts system above.
findings: A day counts toward the streak by reaching the watts goal for that day, the same event that triggers the goal achieved pop up.
We reached the streak through a gym session recorded that day, not by completing a wakeout inside the app.
A longest streak figure is kept separately in the watts stats, alongside the running day count shown on the home screen.
The day off control in settings is framed around not breaking the streak rather than only around pausing notifications.
